Love Bombing.short_definition: Flooding someone with intense affection, praise and attention very early, at a pace that outruns how well the two people actually know each other.
Love Bombing.core_meaning: Flooding someone with intense affection, praise and attention very early, at a pace that outruns how well the two people actually know each other.
Love Bombing.expanded_definition: Love bombing is a burst of adoration at the start of a relationship: constant messages, big declarations, gifts, plans for a shared life, all arriving within days or weeks. Plenty of people fall fast and say so, so speed alone proves little. What marks the pattern is that the intensity is out of step with real knowledge of you, is hard to slow down, and later shifts into coolness, criticism or demands once you have come to depend on it.
Love Bombing.plain_language_summary: Someone showers you with love, praise and big promises far faster than they could really know you, and the warmth later turns out to come with strings.
Love Bombing.why_this_matters: A rush of being adored can feel like finally being seen, so it is easy to let other parts of life shrink around it. If the warmth later cools or gets conditional, you may chase the early version and blame yourself for losing it.
what_it_is: A rapid climb in affection: daily or hourly contact, grand declarations and compliments within the first days or weeks.
Praise that is sweeping rather than specific, such as 'perfect' or 'soulmate', before the person has seen you on a bad day.
Gifts, trips or future plans offered faster than the relationship has had time to earn.
Often paired with a feeling that slowing down would hurt or insult the other person.
Most recognizable in hindsight, when the early intensity is compared with what came after it.
what_it_sounds_like: I knew the first night we talked that you were the one.
I've never felt this way about anyone. Nobody else has ever come close.
Let's get away this weekend, just us. I already booked it.
You don't need to see your friends tonight. Stay with me, I miss you too much.
I think we should move in together. Why wait when we both know?
You're literally perfect. I can't believe you're real.
I'll text you all day, I just can't help myself.
what_it_is_not: Two people who fall quickly and openly for each other, both comfortable with the pace and both able to say 'a bit slower' without it landing as rejection.
A naturally effusive person who is warm and generous with everyone, and has been for years.
A long-distance or whirlwind romance in which fast contact reflects circumstance, such as time zones or a short trip, rather than pressure.
Genuine enthusiasm that settles into steady, ordinary care once the novelty passes, instead of flipping to coldness.
A cultural or family style in which grand romantic language is simply how love is spoken.
this_may_be_it_when: The affection arrives in a rush, then drops sharply after you commit, relax or push back on the pace.
Your attempts to slow down are met with hurt, sulking or the suggestion that you do not feel as deeply as they do.
The praise is generic enough that it could be said to anyone, and it does not change as they learn who you are.
Gifts or sacrifices are mentioned later as a debt you owe.
Your time with friends, family or work quietly shrinks because the contact is so constant.
this_may_not_be_it_when: You can say 'I need to go slower' and the answer is a calm 'okay, thanks for telling me'.
The warmth stays roughly the same through arguments, bad weeks and ordinary boredom.
Their compliments are about particular things you have actually done or said.
Your friendships, hobbies and sleep are intact and they ask about them with interest.
They are equally open about their own flaws and do not treat you as flawless.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Early infatuation is a normal, chemical-feeling stage, and many lasting couples remember it as intense and fast.
Some people text a lot and plan big gestures because that is how they show care.
A person coming out of loneliness may pour out affection with no plan behind it at all.
common_false_positives: A first-love or second-chance romance in which both people are swept up and say so out loud.
A friend who is generous with compliments to everyone in the group.
A partner who was ardent at the start and has since become steadier, which is a usual settling and not a reversal.
discernment_questions: Does the pace feel mutual, or am I mostly trying to keep up with it?
If I asked for a slower speed, what would the reaction tell me?
Do the compliments describe me, or could they describe anybody?
Has this closeness cost me time with other people I care about?
Is the warmth the same on days when I disappoint them?
Would I accept this level of declaration from a coworker I had known for three weeks?
less_concerning_if: You both feel carried along at about the same speed and can talk about it.
Asking for space produces understanding rather than a visible drop in warmth.
The relationship stays steady after the first wave of excitement fades.
more_concerning_if: Big gestures are followed by pressure to commit, move in, share money or drop other plans.
The adoration disappears or turns critical when you set a limit or take time for yourself.
Others who care about you have noticed you pulling away from them since this began.
pattern_over_time_signs: The first weeks are recalled as the best of the relationship, and you find yourself trying to bring them back.
Praise becomes sparser and more tied to what you do for them.
The speed that was exciting at the start now feels like being rushed through decisions.
You keep a mental tally of what they gave you early on, and it makes it harder to object now.
Love Bombing.repair_check: Look for a change in pace that you did not have to fight for: affection that continues at a livable level, interest in who you really are, and room for your other relationships. A promise to 'go back to how it was in the beginning' is not that.
Love Bombing.boundary_respect_check: Ask yourself what happens in the days after you request more space or a slower timeline. If the warmth stays and the request is simply followed, that is a good sign. If it is followed by coldness, guilt or a bigger gesture meant to win you back, note that.
Love Bombing.psychological_mechanism: Intense early attention is unusually rewarding, and expectations often rise to match it. When the warmth later drops or turns conditional, the gap can leave someone working to win back the earlier feeling, while a sense of owing gratitude makes objecting feel ungrateful. Fast closeness also leaves little time for ordinary checking, such as meeting friends or seeing how a partner handles disagreement.
Love Bombing.possible_impact_on_receiver: Some recall being swept off their feet, then feeling bewildered when the tone changed and blaming themselves for the shift. Missing the early weeks the way one misses a place is a common account, as is feeling unable to leave something that once felt like rescue. Embarrassment at having believed it can delay telling friends.

response_options.soft_clarification: Mention the pace without judging it: 'I really like you, and this is moving faster than I'm used to. I'd like us to see each other a couple of times a week for now.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Hold the limit even after a sad or grand reaction: 'I'm not moving in this year. That isn't about how much I care.'
response_options.disengagement: Stop accepting gifts, trips or big commitments for a while, and reply to messages on your own schedule instead of instantly.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell a friend or relative who knew you before this relationship what has been happening, and ask what they have noticed about you since it began.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a manager, client or colleague showers you with sudden praise and favours, note the dates, keep requests in writing, and ask a mentor whether the attention is ordinary for your workplace.

Love Bombing.boundary_script: "I'm enjoying getting to know you, and I want to keep it at a pace where I can still see my friends and sleep normally. Seeing each other twice a week is what works for me right now."
Love Bombing.safety_note: Rapid intensity becomes a safety concern when it comes with pressure to cut off friends, share a home or money, hand over passwords, or when your no is met with anger or threats. Keep your own housing, income and phone access in place early on, and talk to a domestic abuse advocate if anything starts to feel like you cannot say no safely.
misuse_warning: Calling every enthusiastic new partner a love bomber can make ordinary, happy infatuation sound sinister, and it can chill people who are simply open with their feelings.
The label describes a pace and a later change. It is not a way to read someone's motives from their first few weeks of texts.
Love Bombing.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Exclusive Meaning is a specific claim that only this person understands you, which slowly makes other relationships seem lesser, while love bombing is the overall surge of praise and attention. Future Faking centers on promises about what is coming, rather than on affection in the present. Hoovering happens after distance or a breakup, but love bombing arrives at the start of a connection.

Exclusive Meaning.short_definition: Claiming that only this one person truly understands you, which gradually makes everyone else in your life seem less worthy of your trust.
Exclusive Meaning.core_meaning: Claiming that only this one person truly understands you, which gradually makes everyone else in your life seem less worthy of your trust.
Exclusive Meaning.expanded_definition: Exclusive meaning is the repeated message that you are understood by one person alone, and that other people, however close, cannot do it. Said once by a moved partner, it is a romantic line. As a pattern it tends to sit beside small put-downs of your friends or family, and it leaves you with one place to bring your troubles. The difference is whether closeness is described as something added to your life or as a replacement for the rest of it.
Exclusive Meaning.plain_language_summary: One person keeps telling you that nobody else gets you the way they do, and over time your friends and family start to feel like they do not count.
Exclusive Meaning.why_this_matters: If one person becomes the only one who seems to understand you, your other relationships lose weight. That leaves you with fewer people to check reality with, and less ability to leave or disagree safely.
what_it_is: A repeated claim to a special, unmatched understanding of who you are and what you need.
A comparison, stated or implied, in which your other people come out worse: shallow, jealous, not on your side.
Often built from real moments of feeling understood, which makes the claim believable.
Shows up in romance, but also in friendships, mentorships, workplaces and groups with a charismatic leader.
Works gradually, through small remarks, and rarely as one dramatic demand to drop people.
what_it_sounds_like: Your friends don't actually get you. I do.
Nobody has ever listened to you the way I do. You can tell me things you'd never tell your mother.
Why would you talk to her about this? She'll only judge you.
I'm the only person who's ever seen the real you.
They love the version of you that's easy for them. I love all of you.
What we have is on a different level. Other people just can't reach it.
what_it_is_not: Telling someone 'I feel so understood by you', which describes a feeling of closeness without ranking anyone else.
A close confidant, like a best friend or counselor, whom you rely on heavily while still keeping other ties alive and welcome.
A new couple's enthusiasm in the first months, expressed once or twice and then left alone.
Honest concern about a particular friend's behavior, specific and open to your own view of that friend.
A therapist or mentor whose role is to hear you, where the limited scope is clear and everyone else is not put down.
this_may_be_it_when: The remarks about being the only one who gets you come with remarks about specific people who supposedly do not.
You notice you are sharing less with friends because they 'would not see it', in the other person's words.
Your outside relationships are described as threats, competitors or bad influences.
Being understood by them starts to feel like something you must keep earning by staying close.
When you mention a friend's support, the reply is flat, wounded or quickly redirected to themselves.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They encourage you to talk to other people, and are pleased when you feel supported elsewhere.
Their praise for your closeness is a fact about a moment, not a claim that rivals cannot compare.
They speak well of your friends, and ask after them.
You still bring different things to different people and none of it feels guarded.
Their comments about someone in your life are specific, based on something that happened, and not a general verdict.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Early infatuation often produces sentences like 'no one has ever got me like you do' with no hidden aim.
Someone who truly has few friends of their own may overstate how central you are to them out of loneliness.
A deep connection through shared history, such as an illness or a loss, can feel unique and be described that way.
common_false_positives: A spouse of many years who says 'you know me better than anyone', and also gets on well with your sister.
A support group in which people feel understood by others with the same experience, without being told outsiders are lesser.
A teenager and a best friend who say 'only you get me' as part of ordinary adolescence.
discernment_questions: When I say a friend or relative has helped me, how do they respond?
Have I stopped telling others things I used to tell them, and whose idea was that?
Does this person ever suggest another person I could talk to about something?
Is my sense of being understood tied to staying close, agreeing, or avoiding certain people?
If I imagined this person being wrong about my friends, could I say so out loud to them?
less_concerning_if: They are glad when you have other sources of comfort and make room for them.
Compliments about understanding you do not come with criticism of anyone else.
You can disagree with their reading of you and the conversation stays friendly.
more_concerning_if: Specific people in your life are repeatedly described as harmful, with no real examples.
Contact with those people has dropped and you feel unable to bring it back up.
They become distressed or angry when you confide in anyone else.
pattern_over_time_signs: The circle of people you talk to about important things gets smaller month by month.
Your friends remark that they hardly see you, or that you have started echoing the other person's opinions of them.
You begin to censor what you say to others to avoid a cold response at home.
Moments of feeling understood become less frequent, while the claim of understanding gets louder.
Exclusive Meaning.repair_check: Watch whether they begin to treat your other relationships as normal and good, such as asking about your friends, supporting plans with them, and withdrawing earlier digs. An apology that leaves you still expected to bring everything to them has not changed the shape.
Exclusive Meaning.boundary_respect_check: Think about how your last plan with someone else was received. When you set the limit 'I will keep seeing my friends', a respectful answer is simply to let it stand. Sighs, a sudden illness, or a list of that friend's faults are the response worth noticing.
Exclusive Meaning.psychological_mechanism: Feeling deeply understood is one of the most rewarding things in a relationship, so a person may begin to organize their life around the source of it. If the same source also casts other people as lesser, outside views can start to look unreliable, and the person has fewer places to test whether the claim is true. Over time that can narrow where support is sought.
Exclusive Meaning.possible_impact_on_receiver: A pleasant early relief at being known is often followed, in accounts of this pattern, by a quiet loneliness as old friendships thin out. Explaining the relationship to anyone can feel impossible, because each concern seems to confirm that outsiders do not understand. Grief can arrive later, on seeing how much of a life had gone quiet.

response_options.soft_clarification: Say what you notice, once, kindly: 'I like that you get me. I also need my friends, and it hurts when you talk about them as if they don't count.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Keep your plans and your confidences open: 'I'm going to keep talking to my sister about this. You're important to me, and so is she.'
response_options.disengagement: Quietly rebuild contact with one person you have drifted from, even a short call, and notice how the other person reacts to that.
response_options.support_seeking: Pick a friend or relative you have missed and tell them honestly that you have been less in touch than you wanted, and that you would like to change that.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a boss or mentor insists they alone appreciate you, keep up your relationships with peers and other mentors, and ask a trusted colleague what they think of your work.

Exclusive Meaning.boundary_script: "It means a lot that you understand me. I'm still going to spend time with my friends and tell them what's going on in my life, and I'd like that to be okay with you."
Exclusive Meaning.safety_note: Narrowing the people you confide in can be an early part of coercive control, especially when it comes with checking your phone, deciding who you see, or anger when you make plans. Keep at least one outside contact who knows your real situation, and if you are afraid of the reaction, call a domestic violence hotline to talk through options privately.
misuse_warning: Treating any deeply close partner or friend as isolating can punish ordinary intimacy. The question is whether others are being demoted and your access to them reduced, not how close the bond is.
Telling a friend that their partner is doing this, with only a few comments to go on, may make the friend defensive and cut the very connection that helps.
Exclusive Meaning.how_to_distinguish_from_related: The Exception Script tells you that you, unlike everyone around you, are special, which works through flattering comparison to your peers. Exclusive Meaning is about the other person being the sole one who understands you. Love Bombing is the early flood of attention, while exclusive meaning can continue long after the early weeks and grows through small put-downs of the rest of your world.

Conditional Love.short_definition: Offering warmth, approval or affection while you comply with what someone wants, and pulling it back when you decline or disagree.
Conditional Love.core_meaning: Offering warmth, approval or affection while you comply with what someone wants, and pulling it back when you decline or disagree.
Conditional Love.expanded_definition: Conditional love treats affection as a reward and a lever. Care is generous when you comply and noticeably smaller when you disagree, decline or go your own way. It turns up between partners, between parents and children, and in friendships. One sharp comment in a bad moment is common and does not show it. What stands out is a clear, repeated link between obedience and warmth, spoken or obvious to everyone involved.
Conditional Love.plain_language_summary: Someone's warmth and love switch on when you do what they want and switch off when you do not, so love starts to feel like something you must earn.
Conditional Love.why_this_matters: When love depends on pleasing, you learn to scan for the other person's mood and shrink your own needs. Disagreement starts to feel dangerous, and it becomes hard to know what you want separate from what keeps the peace.
what_it_is: Affection, praise or closeness that rises with compliance and falls with disagreement.
A message, spoken or acted out, that love is a payment and that you can fall behind.
Found in couples, in families where approval hangs on grades, looks or obedience, and in friendships with a hidden scorecard.
More than a bad mood: the withdrawal lasts, is tied to a specific request, and ends when you give in.
Sometimes delivered as kindness, such as 'I only want what's best for you', which makes the condition harder to see.
what_it_sounds_like: I could love you so much more if you'd just stop arguing with me.
When you do it my way, we're great. Why can't it always be like that?
I'm not going to be affectionate with someone who talks to me like that.
After everything I do for you, the least you can do is listen.
You're my favorite when you're being agreeable.
Come back to me when you're ready to act right.
what_it_is_not: Saying 'I love you, and I'm very upset about what you did', which keeps care in place while naming the problem.
A reasonable expectation inside a relationship, such as telling the truth or not hitting, where the response is to protect yourself and not to obtain obedience.
A hurt person needing a few hours of distance, who says so and comes back whether or not you give in.
A parent setting a household rule and enforcing a consequence while still showing the child affection.
A heated remark said once during a bad fight and later taken back.
this_may_be_it_when: You can predict the warmth from whether you went along with their wishes that week.
They name the behavior they want as the price of affection.
Once you comply, the affection returns quickly and fully, as if nothing happened.
Your agreeing is described as proof of love, and your declining as proof of the opposite.
You have started to hide opinions or choices to protect the mood.
this_may_not_be_it_when: Their love is stated and shown even when you disagree, for example 'I'm frustrated and I'm not going anywhere'.
They have a bad week and are short with everyone, including when you did nothing.
A request has a real reason, such as your safety or a shared bill, and is not about control.
They apologize for a harsh comment and it does not return.
You feel free to say no and the relationship carries on.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Anyone can be curt or distant when stressed or hurt, and may be less affectionate for a while.
Families often absorb habits of praising achievement, which can feel conditional without anyone planning it that way.
A partner may genuinely struggle to show warmth after a conflict and need time to find it again.
common_false_positives: A friend who is annoyed that you cancelled three times and says so, without threatening the friendship.
A parent who is firm about homework and affectionate at bedtime.
A partner who asks for something reasonable, like telling them when you will be late, and is upset when it does not happen.
discernment_questions: If I said no to this, would the affection survive the week?
Are the conditions ever spoken aloud, or only felt in how the mood changes?
Do I change my choices ahead of time to avoid the withdrawal?
Does the warmth come back as soon as I give in?
Do they place the same conditions on themselves?
less_concerning_if: Disagreement leads to a hard conversation and then ordinary warmth, not a long chill.
The expectations placed on you are ones they hold for themselves too.
You can state a limit and still be treated kindly afterward.
more_concerning_if: Affection is explicitly withheld until you apologize or do what was asked.
The conditions grow over time, covering clothes, friends, work or money.
Other people are told, or shown, that you are difficult whenever you resist.
pattern_over_time_signs: You find yourself pre-editing requests and opinions so as not to trigger the cooling.
The number of things you do not do or say grows quietly.
Good days are tied to compliance, so you start to read the warmth as a grade.
People who knew you earlier say you used to argue more, or laugh more freely.
Conditional Love.repair_check: Repair here looks like warmth that no longer varies with how well you obeyed: they stay kind during a disagreement, name the problem without a chill, and accept a no. A big loving gesture after you gave in just restarts the loop.
Conditional Love.boundary_respect_check: Notice what comes after the first time you decline something they asked for. Warmth that dips for a moment and then returns on its own is ordinary. Warmth that stays away until you apologize or reverse your decision is the part to watch.
Conditional Love.psychological_mechanism: Affection that comes and goes with compliance can work like an intermittent reward, and behavior adjusts fast to protect something valued. Because the wish for love is so basic, a person may begin anticipating the other's preferences before being asked, and may come to experience their own preferences as a risk to the relationship.
Conditional Love.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe walking on eggshells, becoming skilled at reading moods, and feeling guilty for having needs. Some say they could not tell whether they were loved or only managed well. Children who grow up with it sometimes describe adulthood as a hunt for approval, and some partners describe a flat feeling that they are acting a part.

response_options.soft_clarification: Name the link calmly: 'It feels like you're warmer when I agree with you. I'd like us to be able to disagree and still be close.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Refuse the trade: 'I'm not going to change my answer to get you to be kind to me.'
response_options.disengagement: When the chill starts, do not chase it. Do something that is yours for the evening and return to the topic when both of you are calmer.
response_options.support_seeking: Describe two or three specific episodes to a friend or counselor and ask whether the pattern between your choices and their warmth looks as clear to them as it does to you.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a boss rewards agreement and goes cold on dissent, keep your feedback to work content in writing, and seek a mentor outside the reporting line.

Conditional Love.boundary_script: "I want to be close to you, and I also need to be able to say no to things without losing your warmth. I'll talk about this as long as you like, but I won't agree just to keep things pleasant."
Conditional Love.safety_note: On its own, this is a pain in the relationship rather than a physical danger. It becomes a safety matter when withdrawn affection is joined by threats, withheld money or housing, or fear of what happens when you refuse. If you depend on this person for shelter or income, plan with a counselor or advocate before you push back.
misuse_warning: Every relationship has expectations, and holding someone to reasonable ones, such as honesty or respect, is not the same as conditional love. Using the label to dodge fair requests turns it into an excuse.
Applying the term to a parent who disciplines a child, or to anyone who is simply upset, can mislabel normal limits as cruelty.
Conditional Love.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Silent Treatment goes quiet to force a response, while conditional love can be delivered warmly and still tie the warmth to obedience. Negging chips away at your confidence through backhanded remarks and does not require withdrawn affection. Love Bombing hands out affection freely at the start, whereas conditional love measures it out according to your behavior.

Hoovering.short_definition: Reaching out to draw someone back into a relationship after they have pulled away or ended it, often with promises that things will change.
Hoovering.core_meaning: Reaching out to draw someone back into a relationship after they have pulled away or ended it, often with promises that things will change.
Hoovering.expanded_definition: Hoovering, named for the vacuum cleaner, is the pull-back that comes after distance or a breakup: messages, apologies, gifts, sudden crises or declarations of change, sent to restart contact. People do sincerely change and ask for another chance, so a single approach means little. It becomes a pattern when the contact returns after each separation, uses whatever has worked before, and ends up with the old dynamics once you are back.
Hoovering.plain_language_summary: After you pull away or break up, the other person reaches out with promises, apologies or emergencies that draw you back, and the old pattern restarts.
Hoovering.why_this_matters: Each return restarts hope and resets the cycle. You may go back repeatedly, losing time and confidence, and may feel guilty or foolish when it falls apart again.
what_it_is: Contact that arrives after distance or a break, often on or around moments when you have started to settle.
Promises, apologies or declarations of change aimed at the relationship resuming, not at the earlier problem.
Can take many shapes: nostalgic messages, a sudden need for help, a mutual friend carrying a note, a gift, or a claim of illness.
Often repeated across several separations, with the same kinds of approach each time.
Seen mainly in romantic breakups, but also in friendships, family estrangements and former work or group ties.
what_it_sounds_like: I've been in therapy. I'm a different person now. Just let me show you.
I found your old jacket, and the memories came flooding back.
I can't eat or sleep without you. I don't know what I'll do.
Everyone says we belong together. Even my mother asked about you.
I know I messed up. One coffee, that's all I'm asking.
It's your birthday, and I wanted to be the first to say it. Can we talk?
I have something of yours and need to return it. Are you home?
what_it_is_not: A person who truly changed over many months, did the work, and asks once, respectfully, for a chance, then accepts your answer.
Contact required to sort out kids, shared property, a lease or money after a split.
A kind check-in from an ex who marks a loss or a birthday and leaves the response to you.
Reconciliation that both people choose with open eyes and clear terms.
A single message sent in a lonely hour that the person regrets and does not repeat.
this_may_be_it_when: The messages begin soon after you stopped replying, as if timed to the distance.
A no is followed by a new approach through a different route: another number, a friend, a gift to your work.
The promise is about feelings and future, with few concrete steps you can check.
After you return, the earlier problems come back and the promise is no longer mentioned.
The approaches switch between affection, guilt and anger depending on which gets a reply.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They back off when you say you do not want contact.
Evidence of change, such as treatment, steady work on the problem, or months of consistent behavior, comes before any request.
The reason for contact is practical and specific, and ends once handled.
They admit what went wrong in plain terms and do not ask you to forget it.
You decide freely whether and when to respond, and nothing is lost if you do not.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People miss each other after a breakup and may reach out in a weak moment, without calculation.
Some couples do part, reflect, and come back stronger after both put in real work.
Grief and loneliness can produce contact that looks like a pull-back and is simply sadness.
common_false_positives: A former partner who texts once on an anniversary and accepts silence as the reply.
A co-parent contacting you repeatedly about pick-up times.
A friend who drifted away, apologizes sincerely for neglecting you, and lets you choose how much to reconnect.
discernment_questions: Has anything changed that I can see and check, or only what I am told?
How did they respond the last time I said I needed space?
Does the contact come when I seem to be moving on?
Are the same reasons I left still present in how they talk to me now?
What would I decide if I had never been promised anything?
less_concerning_if: They stop when asked and do not send others in their place.
Any change they describe is already visible in their actions over a long time.
The reason for contact is practical and finishes when the task does.
more_concerning_if: The approaches continue after a clear no, or escalate to showing up at your home or workplace.
They rely on your guilt, pity or fear, such as threats of self-harm, to get a reply.
Friends, family or coworkers are being used to pass messages or pressure you.
pattern_over_time_signs: You have separated and reunited several times, each time with a fresh promise.
Each return follows a near-identical script, down to the opening line.
The good stretch after each reunion gets shorter.
You can predict, almost to the week, when the next message will arrive.
Hoovering.repair_check: Real change here is slow and shows up before the request, not after it: months of different behavior, specific accountability for what happened, and no pressure about your timing. A big emotional message with a deadline is the pull itself, not evidence of repair.
Hoovering.boundary_respect_check: A no is the test. Contact that stops when you say you want none is a very different thing from contact that changes channel, tone or messenger. Pay attention to what follows the first clear 'please do not contact me'.
Hoovering.psychological_mechanism: Hope for a better version of someone you care about is powerful, and a sincere-sounding apology can set off relief and attachment even when little has changed. Contact that arrives unpredictably, mixing warmth with distress, can keep attention fixed on the relationship and make a calm decision harder to hold.
Hoovering.possible_impact_on_receiver: A stomach-drop each time a certain name appears on the screen is a common account, along with doubt about whether leaving was right and tiredness from deciding again and again. Going back can bring a sense of having been weak or foolish. After finally not answering, some report a slow calm mixed with grief.

response_options.soft_clarification: State your decision briefly and leave it there: 'I've thought about it and I'm not getting back together. Please don't contact me about this again.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Block or mute the channels they use, and tell mutual friends you will not be relaying messages in either direction.
response_options.disengagement: Do not reply to the emotional content of a message, and do not set a reply time in your head. Silence can be your whole answer.
response_options.support_seeking: Keep a short log of dates and messages and share it with someone who knows the history, so you do not have to re-argue your decision alone each time.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If an ex or former colleague keeps contacting you at work, tell your manager or HR, give them copies of the messages, and ask that the contact be handled through them.

Hoovering.boundary_script: "I read your message. My answer is no, and it won't change with more messages. If there's something practical we need to settle, email me about that only."
Hoovering.safety_note: Repeated unwanted contact after a breakup can slide into stalking, and threats, showing up where you live or work, or messages that mention hurting themselves or you are all danger signals. Save every message, tell someone you trust, and contact a domestic violence advocate or the police if you feel unsafe.
misuse_warning: A former partner who truly has changed and writes once is not hoovering, and branding every attempt at contact that way can shut out honest repair or necessary co-parenting talks.
Labeling a person this way based on one message treats a sad moment as a strategy, which the pattern cannot show.
Hoovering.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Future Faking keeps you waiting inside a relationship that is still going, using promises about what is coming, whereas hoovering reaches for you after you have left or pulled away. Love Bombing floods a new connection with praise. Conditional Love is affection offered only for compliance within the relationship, with no break required.

Future Faking.short_definition: Making vivid promises about a better future together that keep you invested in the present, while the promised things never seem to arrive.
Future Faking.core_meaning: Making vivid promises about a better future together that keep you invested in the present, while the promised things never seem to arrive.
Future Faking.expanded_definition: Future faking uses promised milestones, such as marriage, a home, a trip, a changed habit or a finished project, to keep a person patient with how things are now. Real plans do slip, and honest people miss dates. Concern grows when the promises are large and detailed, the dates keep moving, nothing small gets done meanwhile, and your waiting is asked to stand in for the thing itself.
Future Faking.plain_language_summary: Someone describes a wonderful future with you in detail, so you keep waiting and putting up with the present, but the promises keep sliding away.
Future Faking.why_this_matters: Waiting on a promise can use up years, savings or other options. When the future never comes, you may also doubt your own judgment for having believed it, which makes the next decision harder.
what_it_is: Specific, appealing promises about a future that depends on you staying: a wedding, children, a move, a job, a change in the other person.
A pattern where the date keeps shifting, and each delay arrives with a fresh reason and a fresh promise.
Stands in for present action: talk about the house rather than saving for it, talk about quitting drinking rather than seeking help.
Most convincing when it touches the thing you most want.
Appears in romance, but also in jobs ('a promotion is coming'), friendships and business ventures.
what_it_sounds_like: Once the divorce is final, we'll get married. I promise it won't be long.
We'll buy the house by next spring. I've already picked out the street.
After this project, I'll have time for us. Just hang in there.
I'm going to quit drinking after the holidays. This time I mean it.
Give it a year and you'll see. I'm going to make it all up to you.
I'll introduce you to my family once things calm down.
We'll have the baby when the money situation is sorted.
what_it_is_not: A sincere plan delayed by a layoff, illness or family emergency, where the person says so honestly and adjusts the plan with you.
A hopeful dream shared in conversation that was never offered as a promise or a reason for you to wait.
A couple jointly deciding to put off a goal until they can afford it, with both agreeing on the timeline.
A person who keeps small promises each week and also speaks about larger hopes for the years ahead.
A promise that does come true, even later than first hoped.
this_may_be_it_when: The promised date has moved more than once, each time with a new explanation.
There are no visible steps toward the promise, only talk about it.
The promise comes up most when you voice doubt, complain or talk about leaving.
You are being asked to give up something real now, such as time, money or an opportunity, on the strength of it.
Small commitments today, like returning a call or showing up on time, are also not kept.
this_may_not_be_it_when: You can see real progress, like savings accounts opened, applications filed, or treatment attended.
They tell you plainly when a plan has slipped and what that means for you.
You are not asked to put anything on hold while waiting.
They are open to you deciding not to wait and do not use the promise to discourage this.
Outside events that anyone could verify explain the delay.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Optimistic people underestimate how long things take and promise in good faith.
Hard circumstances, such as visa waits, court dates, illness or job loss, can push back real plans.
People sometimes say big, warm things in the moment out of affection, without having planned the details.
common_false_positives: A partner who says they want to marry you, saves for the ring, and sets a date together with you.
A manager who says a promotion depends on budget approval, and tells you when the decision is made.
A friend who says 'we should travel someday' and does not mean it as a pledge.
discernment_questions: What have they actually done toward this promise in the past six months?
What am I being asked to give up or wait for while it happens?
How many times has the date changed?
Do they keep small promises, like showing up when they said they would?
If nothing ever changed from today, would I still want to be here?
less_concerning_if: The delay has a real, checkable cause and you were told promptly.
Concrete steps are happening in view, alongside the talk.
You are free to make your own plans without being talked out of them.
more_concerning_if: You have made major life decisions, like leaving a job or lending money, based on the promise.
Questions about the timeline are met with irritation, hurt or the suggestion that you do not trust them.
The promise grows bigger exactly when you are close to leaving.
pattern_over_time_signs: You can list several promised milestones, none of which has arrived.
The explanations vary but the outcome is the same.
You stop asking about the date because the answer is always 'soon'.
Your own plans, savings or opportunities have been shelved to leave room for theirs.
Future Faking.repair_check: Repair means the promise becomes smaller, dated and checkable: one concrete step done this month, and an honest account of what was not done before. A fresh, bigger vision of the future given after you complain is more of the same.
Future Faking.boundary_respect_check: Ask for a specific step and a date, then watch what comes next. A person may be unable to deliver, yet still work out a first step with you. A reply made entirely of warm words about how much you matter, with the step left out, is a different response.
Future Faking.psychological_mechanism: A vivid, hoped-for future can feel almost real, and the more of it has been imagined and told to others, the harder it is to stop investing. Each new promise can reset the wait. The more time or money already spent, the harder it gets to stop and count the cost.
Future Faking.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe years of 'almost', holding their breath for a date, and anger at themselves when it passes. Some talk about having postponed their own education, children, or moves for someone else's timetable. Others say the hardest part was grieving a future that existed only in conversation.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask for specifics, kindly: 'I like that picture. What is the first step, and when do you think it can happen?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Tie your own decisions to what has already happened: 'I'm not going to leave my job or sign anything until the plan is in motion.'
response_options.disengagement: Stop adjusting your life around the promise. Put your own plans and savings back on your own calendar.
response_options.support_seeking: Write down the promises with dates and show them to someone you trust, asking what they notice when they see the list as a whole.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a promotion or raise keeps being deferred, ask for the terms in an email, and keep that email. Check what the written policy or contract says.

Future Faking.boundary_script: "I believe you want that future. I need to see the first step before I change anything in my own plans. Can we agree on one thing you'll do this month?"
Future Faking.safety_note: Future faking is usually a slow drain rather than a danger. It becomes a serious concern when the promise is tied to marriage for immigration status, a loan, a shared lease, or signing over money or property. In those cases, talk to a legal aid service or financial counselor before you commit anything in writing.
misuse_warning: Delayed plans are common, so calling every unmet promise 'future faking' treats a hard year as a con. The label needs a record of shifting dates and missing steps.
Using it to guess that someone never meant a promise claims knowledge of their mind that nobody outside it has.
Future Faking.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Hoovering pulls you back after you have left, using promises, whereas future faking keeps you in a relationship that is still going. Love Bombing floods the present with affection and praise; future faking mostly talks about a later time. Conditional Love ties affection to obedience, and future faking ties your patience to a payoff that never comes.

Negging.short_definition: Slipping in a subtle insult, wrapped as a compliment or a joke, so that you feel a little smaller and a little more eager for approval.
Negging.core_meaning: Slipping in a subtle insult, wrapped as a compliment or a joke, so that you feel a little smaller and a little more eager for approval.
Negging.expanded_definition: A neg is a remark that looks like praise but carries a dig: a compliment with a catch, surprise that you did well, a joke about a feature you are sensitive about. Awkward people and teasing friends say clumsy things too, so one comment tells you little. Repetition is what changes things: digs that come regularly, land on insecure spots, are followed by warmth, and leave you working harder for a better one.
Negging.plain_language_summary: Someone mixes small put-downs into their compliments, so you end up feeling a bit worse about yourself and a bit more eager to win their approval.
Negging.why_this_matters: Small digs add up. Over weeks you may begin to trust the other person's opinion of you above your own, and work hard for compliments that always come with a sting.
what_it_is: A remark that praises and cuts in the same sentence, often with a 'for you' or 'considering' attached.
Aimed at something you are already unsure of, such as looks, intelligence, class, age or career.
Delivered in a light, joking or even affectionate tone, which makes objecting feel petty.
Often followed by real warmth, so that approval feels precious and a bit unpredictable.
Common in dating and flirting, but also seen at work, in families and among friends.
what_it_sounds_like: You're pretty smart for someone who didn't go to college.
That dress is bold. Most people couldn't pull it off, but you do you.
I'm surprised you finished that so fast. Good for you!
You'd be gorgeous if you smiled more. Seriously, it's a shame.
Wow, you actually cooked this? Not bad!
I like that you don't care what people think of how you look.
Not many guys with your job would be this thoughtful.
what_it_is_not: Mutual, playful teasing between people who both enjoy it and would both stop if one asked.
An awkward compliment from someone who is clumsy with words and winces when you point it out.
Honest, kind feedback about a mistake, aimed at the work and offered to help.
A cultural or family style of ribbing that everyone in the group takes in fun.
A compliment that surprised you because it was higher than you expected from yourself, not because of a dig.
this_may_be_it_when: The sting always lands on a tender spot you have mentioned or shown.
The compliment only works if you accept a small insult with it.
When you react, you are told you are too sensitive or cannot take a joke.
You notice a pull to prove them wrong, followed by relief when they approve.
The comments are mostly made in front of others, or when you were doing well.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They stop and apologize when you say a comment stung.
They tease themselves in the same way.
Their praise, when it comes, has no tag line.
The same remark would have been fine from a friend of equal standing and you find it funny too.
It happened once and has not come up again.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Many people are bad at giving compliments and tack on qualifiers out of nerves.
Banter between close friends often includes teasing that is meant and received as affection.
Surprise at your success can be a plain expression of admiration, clumsily put.
common_false_positives: A sibling who has roasted you since childhood and cheers loudest at your wedding.
A colleague whose blunt phrasing, such as 'that's better than I expected', is how they praise everyone.
A date who jokes about their own flaws and then jokes about yours, lightly, while both of you laugh.
discernment_questions: After this person compliments me, do I feel better or slightly worse?
If a friend told me the same words, would I hear a compliment?
Do the digs land on things I have said I am sensitive about?
Do I find myself working harder to hear something kind from them?
When I say it hurt, is it taken seriously?
less_concerning_if: The comment came once, and they changed course when told.
The teasing flows both ways and is about a variety of subjects.
You leave most conversations feeling at least as good about yourself as when you arrived.
more_concerning_if: The remarks come steadily and cluster around your most insecure points.
Objecting is treated as proof that you are fragile.
Your confidence and your wish for their approval have both risen noticeably since you met.
pattern_over_time_signs: You start double-checking your outfit, answers or work before you see them.
You tell a story of their approval as a prize you won last week.
Friends comment that you seem more nervous or self-critical lately.
You laugh at jokes about yourself that you would not have accepted a year ago.
Negging.repair_check: Repair would be that the comments stop landing on the same spots, they give plain compliments that need no footnote, and they take it seriously when you say a remark hurt. Switching to heavier praise for a while after you object is not the same as changing.
Negging.boundary_respect_check: Notice the next remark once you have called a comment a dig. If it is quieter, kinder and not repeated, the message got through. If you hear 'I was only joking' followed by a similar line, the boundary was heard and set aside.
Negging.psychological_mechanism: Mixed messages, a lift and a drop in the same sentence, hold attention longer than plain praise or plain criticism. A slightly unsure person may then work to secure approval that has been made to seem scarce. Because the sting is phrased as a joke, objecting can look like the bigger offense.
Negging.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe replaying a comment for days, wondering whether they were being silly to mind, and slowly starting to dress, speak or work for one person's reaction. Some say they became quieter around that person, or began checking themselves in mirrors. Others recall laughing along while feeling a small drop in their stomach.

response_options.soft_clarification: Reflect the comment back lightly: 'Did you mean that as a compliment? It sounded like there was a catch.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Draw a line without raising your voice: 'I don't like jokes about my appearance. Please skip those.'
response_options.disengagement: Respond to a backhanded line with a flat 'okay' and a new topic, and spend less time in settings where it is a regular feature.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell a friend the exact words used and ask how they sound. A second reader often hears the sting you have been explaining away.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a colleague or boss makes digs in meetings, note dates and words, respond to the work content only, and bring repeated remarks to HR or a manager you trust.

Negging.boundary_script: "When you say I'm smart for someone like me, it doesn't sound like a compliment to me. If you want to compliment me, just say the nice part."
Negging.safety_note: Negging by itself is a corrosive habit rather than a danger. It would change if the remarks escalate to threats, to comments about your body that become touching you without consent, or to attempts to make you dependent on someone with power over your job or housing. In that case, document what was said and speak to HR, a union rep or a trusted advocate.
misuse_warning: Ordinary teasing and clumsy compliments are common, and calling each one a neg can end friendly banter or make an awkward person seem sinister.
The word is also a name from pickup-artist culture, so using it about someone you know as a charge of scheming goes beyond what the words alone can show.
Negging.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Conditional Love holds back warmth until you comply, while negging delivers digs and warmth at the same time. Exclusive Meaning tells you only they understand you, a message of closeness; negging lowers your standing. The Exception Script flatters by setting you above others, while negging lowers you in the same breath as it praises you.

Silent Treatment.short_definition: Withholding all communication from someone, with no stated end, until they apologize or give way to what the other person wants.
Silent Treatment.core_meaning: Withholding all communication from someone, with no stated end, until they apologize or give way to what the other person wants.
Silent Treatment.expanded_definition: The silent treatment is a stretch of deliberate non-response: no answers, no eye contact, messages left unread, a person who is in the room treated as absent. Everyone goes quiet sometimes, and taking time to cool down is ordinary. What changes the meaning is that the silence has no end date, is aimed at one person, and lifts only when that person apologizes or complies. It tells the person that closeness is switched off until they fix it.
Silent Treatment.plain_language_summary: Someone stops talking to you on purpose, with no end in sight, until you apologize or give in. The quiet itself is the pressure.
Silent Treatment.why_this_matters: Being frozen out hurts in a way the body treats as real pain. The open-ended wait can leave you desperate to end it at any cost, apologizing for things you do not think were wrong.
what_it_is: A deliberate stop to talking, replying or acknowledging someone, with no stated end.
Often shows up as ignored texts, one-word answers, leaving the room, or speaking to everyone else but you.
Ends when the other person apologizes, gives in, or performs some act of making up.
Aimed at one person and often at the moment they raise a complaint or make a choice.
Can last hours, days or weeks, and appears in couples, families, friendships and workplaces.
what_it_sounds_like: Nothing. No reply for two days after you asked a question.
I'm not talking to you until you admit what you did.
A flat 'fine' and a walk out of the room, then no words for the evening.
Don't speak to me. You know what you did.
Messages read, with no answer, while they chat happily with others.
Talking to the dog and the kids but never to you.
what_it_is_not: Saying 'I'm too angry to talk about this right now. Can we pick it up after dinner?', which has a reason and a return time.
A person who goes quiet from shutting down, depression or overwhelm, and who is silent with everyone and not just you.
A break agreed on by both people during a heated argument, with a time to return.
Taking space after a hard day, announced plainly, and not tied to anything you must do.
Quiet from someone whose communication style is slow or private, and who has always been that way.
this_may_be_it_when: The silence starts right after you disagree or set a limit, and never has a stated end.
They speak normally to everyone else in the room.
It ends only after you apologize, bring a peace offering, or drop the issue.
You are expected to work out what you did wrong without being told.
Once the silence breaks, the original problem is never discussed.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They said they needed time and gave a time when they would return, and did.
The quiet is not specific to you and shows up in all their relationships.
They come back to talk the issue through, and do not require an apology first.
You feel free to approach them and they answer, even if briefly.
They are unwell, grieving or exhausted, and the quiet is clearly about that.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Many people need quiet to settle down after conflict, and may not have the words yet.
Some people shut down when flooded with emotion and cannot talk, whatever their wish.
Phones die, work gets busy, and a slow reply is often just a slow reply.
common_false_positives: A partner who says 'I need an hour' and then returns to talk.
A teenager who gives short answers for a week while stressed about school, and does so with everyone.
A friend who is late to reply because of a hard stretch, and apologizes warmly when they resurface.
discernment_questions: Was a reason or a return time given, or did it simply start?
Does the silence lift only when I apologize or give in?
Do they speak freely to others during the same period?
Once talk resumes, do we ever address what the silence was about?
Do I find myself apologizing for things I do not believe I did wrong, just to end it?
less_concerning_if: The quiet is brief, announced and followed by a real conversation.
It is not aimed at you alone and does not need your apology to end.
They can describe afterward what they were feeling.
more_concerning_if: It lasts days or weeks and cuts off practical things, like telling you about money, kids or housing.
It comes with other signs of control, like checking where you are or anger when you try to reach them.
You have started agreeing to things you disagree with to avoid the next one.
pattern_over_time_signs: You can predict that a disagreement about a certain subject will end in days of silence.
You avoid raising issues because of what will follow.
You are the one who always breaks the silence first.
The stretches get longer, or happen with smaller triggers than before.
Silent Treatment.repair_check: Repair would be that they talk with you about the silence itself afterward, say what they needed, and next time give a reason and time to return. Warmth that simply resumes with no mention of what happened leaves the pattern untouched.
Silent Treatment.boundary_respect_check: Over several rounds, one question tells you more than any single reply. When you have said you will talk but will not be ignored for days, does the next fight end with a spoken pause and a return, or with another stretch of nothing?
Silent Treatment.psychological_mechanism: Being ignored by someone you depend on can set off a strong threat response, and the urge to end that discomfort quickly can override your own view. Without information about why or for how long, the mind may fill in the worst, and apologizing can start to feel like the only exit.
Silent Treatment.possible_impact_on_receiver: A knot in the stomach, constant phone checking, rehearsed apologies and a feeling of being invisible come up often in accounts of being frozen out. Some start to doubt whether they did something terrible, and resentment can sit beside fear of the next freeze. Children subjected to it often say love felt revocable.

response_options.soft_clarification: Leave one open door in writing: 'I can see you need space. I'm here when you're ready to talk, and I'd like to know roughly when that might be.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Decline to bargain with the quiet: 'I'm not going to apologize for something I don't think I did wrong just to end the silence.'
response_options.disengagement: Do not chase, plead or send a stream of messages. Go about your day, keep your routines, and let a single calm message stand.
response_options.support_seeking: Do not carry the freeze alone. Call a friend, and describe how long it has been and what it was about, and notice how they react to the details.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a colleague or manager freezes you out, keep communicating about the work in writing, document that essential information was withheld, and take repeated cases to HR.

Silent Treatment.boundary_script: "I'm happy to talk about what happened, and I understand if you need a few hours first. I can't keep going when I'm met with days of silence. Tell me when you'll be ready."
Silent Treatment.safety_note: On its own, silence is a painful pressure and not a physical threat. It matters more when you depend on the person for housing, money or care and the freeze cuts off practical information, or when it alternates with intimidation. If any of that is present, make sure you have a separate plan, such as your own funds and a trusted contact, and consider talking to a counselor.
misuse_warning: Needing space is healthy and many people go quiet from overwhelm, so labeling any pause as 'the silent treatment' can punish someone for self-regulating, especially if they have a neurodivergent or shutdown response.
Demanding an immediate response and then calling its absence abuse can become a form of pressure of its own.
Silent Treatment.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Conditional Love is the broader link between your obedience and warmth, which can happen with plenty of talking; the silent treatment is that link expressed as total non-communication. Negging keeps up contact and lowers your confidence through digs. Hoovering is contact that returns after a break, while the silent treatment is contact withdrawn within a relationship that continues.

The Exception Script.short_definition: Telling you that you are uniquely different from everyone else around you, so that keeping that special status depends on staying close to the speaker.
The Exception Script.core_meaning: Telling you that you are uniquely different from everyone else around you, so that keeping that special status depends on staying close to the speaker.
The Exception Script.expanded_definition: The exception script is flattery built on contrast: you are not like your peers, family, other students or other employees, you are the one who truly gets it. It can feel wonderful, especially if you have felt overlooked. The difficulty is that the praise has a silent condition. To stay the exception, you may need to keep your distance from the very people you were set apart from, and to avoid questioning the speaker.
The Exception Script.plain_language_summary: Someone tells you that you are special and unlike all the others, and over time staying special seems to mean keeping away from your peers and not disagreeing with them.
The Exception Script.why_this_matters: Being singled out can feel like being seen. But when your specialness depends on separating from peers or never questioning one person, you can lose your allies and your own judgment without noticing.
what_it_is: Praise that works by comparison: you are better, deeper or more mature than the people around you.
A private status offered by someone with some power or influence, such as an older partner, a teacher, a boss, a coach or a group leader.
Often accompanied by quiet criticism of the very peers you are being separated from, which makes them look like a lesser group.
A condition that is felt rather than spoken: stepping back into your group or questioning the speaker risks losing the special place.
Particularly strong with people who feel misunderstood, new, or on the edge of a group.
what_it_sounds_like: You're not like the other girls on the team. You actually take this seriously.
Honestly, you're the only one here with any real talent.
You're so mature for your age. The kids in your class wouldn't get you.
The others don't see what you see. That's what makes you different.
I don't tell this to just anyone. You're special.
Don't tell the rest of them what I said. They'd be jealous.
You're better than your friends, you know that? You deserve people on your level.
what_it_is_not: Specific praise for something you actually did, such as 'your analysis of the data was the strongest in the group'.
A teacher or mentor who sees promise in you and also encourages you to share it and learn from peers.
Being chosen for a role on merit, which is stated openly and is the same for others in your position.
A friend who says 'you're the one I call when things get hard', a statement of closeness that leaves your other ties alone.
A compliment about being different in a way you enjoy, such as being a bookworm in a sporty family, with no one placed beneath you.
this_may_be_it_when: The compliment depends on others looking worse.
You are asked to keep the praise or the relationship secret from peers or family.
Your specialness seems to be at risk whenever you disagree or spend time with your group.
The speaker's comments about your peers have become sharper since you got close.
You find yourself pulling away from people who used to matter to you, feeling above them.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The praise is about specific work and could be repeated in front of everyone.
They encourage you to include your peers and mention their strengths too.
You can disagree with them and still be valued.
The attention is open, such as a public award, and open to question by others.
They treat other people in your position with similar respect.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Good teachers and coaches do notice talent and may single someone out to challenge them.
A friend may admire how you differ from a group, such as your humor, without wanting anything.
Being praised by a respected person can feel exclusive simply because they have only said it to you.
common_false_positives: A professor who says your essay stood out and suggests you apply for an honors program open to anyone.
A grandparent who calls you their favorite reader in the family and says it to each grandchild.
A new partner who admires your independence and is glad for you to keep your friends.
discernment_questions: Is the praise about what I did, or about how I compare with other people?
Am I asked to keep it quiet, or to stay away from certain people?
What happens to the warmth when I side with my peers or disagree?
Would I be comfortable with my friends or parents hearing exactly what they say about me?
Has my view of the people around me grown colder since this began?
less_concerning_if: The praise is public, specific and offered to others who earn it too.
You are encouraged to bring your peers along and keep your friendships.
You can question them without a drop in regard.
more_concerning_if: The attention comes with secrecy, private contact, gifts or a request that you not mention it to others.
The speaker has authority over you, such as a boss, teacher, coach or an adult when you are a teen.
Your peers are described as jealous or hostile, and you feel increasingly separate from them.
pattern_over_time_signs: You spend less time with the group you were set apart from, and see them as lesser.
You find it harder to criticize the speaker, even privately.
The sense of being chosen becomes an important part of how you see yourself.
Friends or family say they have noticed you have changed, or seem to be keeping something from them.
The Exception Script.repair_check: Look for praise that no longer needs a contrast: specific, shared with others, and given with no expectation of secrecy or distance. They also begin to welcome your peers into the picture. A bigger helping of flattery after you start pulling away is the same script with the volume up.
The Exception Script.boundary_respect_check: Try mentioning the praise to a friend, or inviting a peer along, and watch what happens. Easy acceptance suggests the attention was ordinary. Annoyance, requests for secrecy or a sudden coolness when you act like part of the group tells you something about the condition attached.
The Exception Script.psychological_mechanism: Feeling special meets a deep need to be seen, and people can become attached to a source of that feeling. If the status is framed as depending on being unlike others, a person may protect it by distancing from peers and avoiding disagreement, since both seem to threaten the special place. That can reduce the outside perspectives that would otherwise check the relationship.
The Exception Script.possible_impact_on_receiver: A warm glow, gradually mixed with worry about losing the status, is typical of what is reported, along with feeling above or apart from peers and later loneliness once friendships have drifted. Confusion and betrayal can follow on finding others were told the same thing. Shame at having felt superior is also named.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask for the specifics: 'What did I do that you liked? I'd like to hear about the work, not just how I compare with others.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Decline the contrast: 'I don't want to be put above the others. They're good at things too, and I'd rather not hear them criticized.'
response_options.disengagement: Step back from private, one-on-one praise and keep contact with this person to open, group or work settings.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell a parent, friend or colleague you trust exactly what has been said and whether you were asked to keep it quiet. Secrecy is the part worth saying out loud.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a boss or senior colleague builds you up against your team, keep feedback in writing, share credit openly, and ask a mentor or HR how the favor will be seen if it is later withdrawn.

The Exception Script.boundary_script: "Thank you, but I don't want to be told I'm better than my friends. Tell me what you think I did well, and I'm going to keep sharing it with the people around me."
The Exception Script.safety_note: When someone with power over you, especially an adult with a young person, singles you out and asks for secrecy, gifts, private messaging or time alone, that can be a warning sign of grooming or exploitation. Tell a parent, school counselor or other trusted adult, and contact child protection services or the police if you or a young person you know feels unsafe.
misuse_warning: Good mentors and teachers often notice and encourage special ability. Assuming that any praise for a student or employee is a script can discourage people who are offering honest encouragement.
Telling someone who feels proud of a real talent that they were only flattered can feel like a dismissal of their achievement.
The Exception Script.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Exclusive Meaning claims that only the speaker understands you, centered on their unique bond with you. The Exception Script praises you by setting you apart from your peers. Love Bombing is a flood of attention and affection in a romantic or close bond, while the exception script can be calm and quiet, in any setting where someone has influence over you.
